title: Immigration: Open Borders vs. Restriction
scope: How many people a state admits and on what terms. Admission, not integration.

overview.summary: Admission as a right migrants hold, a bargain states strike, or a sovereign choice: the fight is over who the border serves.
overview.scope_covered: Who a state may admit or exclude: freedom of movement, selection criteria, wage and fiscal effects, asylum duty, cohesion, origin-country effects.
overview.scope_excluded: Internal migration and displacement, naturalization and citizenship law, enforcement and detention practice, integration program design.
overview.why_now: The EU’s asylum pact became fully applicable on 12 June 2026: shared screening and border procedures, plus a solidarity mechanism every member state must contribute to, though each may send money or staff rather than accept a single relocated asylum seeker. Hungary rejects both of the mechanism’s main options, mandatory relocation quotas and financial contributions, and says it will accept only technical assistance, and only with the approval of frontline states.

stats.label: International migrants worldwide · UN estimate
stats.note: That is 3.7% of the world’s population, up only modestly from 2.9% in 1990 even as the absolute number nearly doubled.
stats.detail: The UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs periodically re-estimates the global migrant stock from national censuses and population registers. Its 2024 edition, released in January 2025, counts 304 million people living outside their country of birth, nearly double the 154 million estimated for 1990. Over the same period their share of world population rose from 2.9% to 3.7%, an increase the Population Division describes as only modest.
stats.source_label: UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs, International Migrant Stock 2024

stats.label: Adults who would migrate permanently if they could · Gallup
stats.note: Roughly 900 million adults, down in 2025 from the record 16% that held every year from 2021 through 2024.
stats.detail: Gallup’s World Poll asks a representative sample of adults whether they would like to move permanently to another country if they could. The 2025 wave, based on about 144,000 interviews across 139 countries and areas, found 15%, or roughly 900 million people, would: a one-point fall from the 16% recorded each year from 2021 through 2024. It is useful context for how large migration flows could plausibly become under much more open policy, though wanting to move is not the same as being able or intending to actually do it.

stats.label: Wage effect of immigration on the average native-born worker · long run
stats.note: Wages barely move over 10+ years; declines fall on earlier immigrants and workers without a diploma.
stats.detail: A National Academies of Sciences synthesis of the empirical literature found little evidence that immigration affects overall native-born wages or employment once the economy has had time to adjust. The two groups most likely to see a measurable wage effect are prior immigrants and native-born workers without a high school diploma, who compete most directly with new low-skilled arrivals; native teen employment rates are largely unaffected, though hours worked can fall. Higher-skilled immigration shows positive wage spillovers for some native workers.
stats.source_label: National Academies of Sciences, The Economic and Fiscal Consequences of Immigration

stats.label: People forcibly displaced worldwide · UNHCR
stats.note: Most have never crossed a border: 68.7 million are displaced inside their own country, versus 41.6 million refugees and others needing protection.
stats.detail: The 117.8 million comprises 68.7 million people displaced by conflict or violence inside their own country (a matter for their own state rather than international asylum law), 41.6 million refugees and others in need of international protection (including Palestinians registered with UNRWA) and 9 million asylum seekers with a claim still pending. Those categories sum to more than the total because internally displaced Palestine refugees appear in two of them and are counted only once in the 117.8 million. The total is down from 123.2 million at the end of 2024, a fall UNHCR attributes to a sharp rise in returns, mostly to Afghanistan, Syria and Sudan.
stats.source_label: UNHCR, Global Trends: Forced Displacement in 2025

stats.label: Potential world GDP gain from open labor mobility · economists’ models
stats.note: Four stylized models of a barrier-free world, not policy forecasts: gains far above those from freeing trade or capital, with a spread that turns on their assumptions.
stats.detail: A widely cited 2011 survey by economist Michael Clemens compared four models of the world economy estimating the world GDP gain from eliminating migration barriers entirely: 147% (Hamilton and Whalley, 1984), 122% (Klein and Ventura, 2007), 97% (Moses and Letnes, 2004) and 67% (Iregui, 2005), all inside the commonly quoted 50 to 150 percent range. Clemens notes the exact magnitudes are highly sensitive to modeling assumptions, among them how productive migrants would be at the destination and how much emigration is politically feasible, and argues the existing evidence gives little reason to believe the numbers greatly overstate the gains. In his 2014 book Immigration Economics, George Borjas reads the same assumption the other way: gains this large require billions of people to move without bringing the institutions and norms that kept their origin countries poor, and he calls it inconceivable that the North’s infrastructure would remain unchanged after the admission of billions of new workers. Either way, these are stylized modeling exercises, not policy forecasts for any actual proposal on the table.

stats.label: Age above which the native-born cost government more than immigrants · US data
stats.note: Immigrants pay in less during their working years, but past about 60 the native-born cost government more per person, driven by Social Security and Medicare use.
stats.detail: Measured across federal, state and local budgets together, the National Academies found the per-person net fiscal balance of the native-born turning less favorable than that of the foreign-born at around age 60, driven by heavier use of Social Security and Medicare in later life, with the US-born children of immigrants the exception to that pattern. The same 2016 synthesis found immigrants’ net fiscal impact is generally positive at the federal level and generally negative at the state and local level, largely because education is a local cost while many benefits of a larger, younger workforce accrue nationally. Second-generation adults, the US-born children of immigrants, were found to be among the strongest net fiscal contributors of any group, ahead of both first-generation immigrants and other native-born Americans, though results depend heavily on assumptions about how to allocate shared public goods like national defense.
stats.source_label: National Academies of Sciences, The Economic and Fiscal Consequences of Immigration

stats.label: Diversity’s measured association with social trust · meta-analysis of 87 studies
stats.note: Close to zero on a scale where 1 would be a perfect link: pooling 1,001 estimates from 87 studies finds a small negative association, with the size, the geography and the mechanism still argued over.
stats.detail: Robert Putnam’s 2007 study, drawing on a survey of roughly 30,000 US respondents including samples from 41 communities, found ethnic diversity associated with lower trust both between and within ethnic groups even after controls, and coined the phrase “hunkering down.” Replications have not all agreed: a 2011 British study by Sturgis, Brunton-Smith, Read and Allum, using multilevel models on a sample approaching 25,000, found no effect of ethnic diversity on generalized trust, and an association with what the authors call strategic trust that was statistically significant but, in their own terms, trivial next to the effects of economic deprivation and of how socially connected people were. Pooling the field, Dinesen, Schaeffer and Sønderskov report a partial correlation of -0.0256 (standard error 0.0044) across 1,001 estimates from 87 studies: negative and statistically significant, but in their own description rather modest, and conditioning on covariates changes it only slightly. What stays disputed is magnitude, geography and mechanism: neighborhood versus national, short run versus long run, and whether the association tracks diversity itself or the poverty and segregation that often travel with it.
stats.source_label: Dinesen, Schaeffer and Sønderskov, Annual Review of Political Science

stats.label: International migrant workers worldwide · International Labour Organization estimate
stats.note: Migrant workers make up 4.7% of the global labor force; most cross-border migration is labor migration, not forced displacement.
stats.detail: The ILO counted 167.7 million international migrant workers in destination-country labor forces in 2022, 4.7% of the global labor force, a narrower slice than the 304 million global migrant stock since not every migrant works or seeks work abroad. This is the population that points-based and employer-sponsored selection systems are trying to manage.
stats.source_label: International Labour Organization, Global Estimates on International Migrant Workers, 4th edition

stats.label: Remittances to low- and middle-income countries · World Bank
stats.note: Money migrants send home now outpaces foreign direct investment and foreign aid to these countries combined, though how far it offsets the skills those countries lose is disputed.
stats.detail: The World Bank and KNOMAD estimate remittance flows to low- and middle-income countries at about $685 billion in 2024, a total that has grown in most years for two decades and now outpaces foreign direct investment and official development assistance combined; over the past decade remittances rose 57% while foreign direct investment fell 41%. It is the main channel through which migration is argued to benefit origin countries directly, though how much it offsets the lost labor and skills of the people who left is debated.

stats.label: US foreign-born share of population · Census and Pew
stats.note: About 51.9 million people as of mid-2025, more immigrants in absolute terms than any other single country hosts.
stats.detail: As of June 2025, 51.9 million immigrants lived in the United States, 15.4% of the total population. The US hosts more immigrants in absolute numbers than any other country (Germany is second, at roughly 17 million as of 2024), though several other high-income countries have a higher foreign-born share. The June 2025 figure is down from a record 53.3 million, or 15.8% of the population, in January 2025, the highest share Pew records and the start of the first decline in the US foreign-born population since the 1960s.
stats.source_label: Pew Research Center, analysis of US Census Bureau data

questions.text: Does where a person happens to be born justify limiting where they may live and work?
questions.why: Turns on whether birthplace is a morally arbitrary trait like race, or a citizenship claim that grounds real duties and rights of self-governing peoples.
questions.detail:
The case that birthplace cannot justify the limit draws on liberal equality: birthplace is as unchosen as race or sex, traits rejected elsewhere as grounds for withholding rights, so the sheer gap in life chances a border creates for identical work and identical effort reads as an unjustified allocation rather than a natural fact. On this view, treating a border as morally different from any other accident of birth needs an argument, and none of the usual candidates (national culture, prior residence, a vote never taken by the person excluded) survives scrutiny.

The case that birthplace does justify the limit reframes the question away from individual desert and toward what political membership is: rights and obligations arise from belonging to a bounded, self-governing community, not from a free-floating cosmopolitan ledger, so a state’s control over admission is closer to a family’s or a club’s right to define itself than to a caste rule imposed on people who never had a say. David Miller carries the point into policy: a democracy may limit numbers to protect the mutual trust and the shared culture its self-government runs on, and what separates a bounded community from a caste is the obligation it accepts toward those it does admit, substantially equal rights and a route to full citizenship.

questions.text: Where does the obligation to shelter people fleeing danger stop, and who gets to draw that line?
questions.why: International law bars returning people to danger but is silent on how many claims a state must hear, how strictly danger is defined, and who judges a claim false.
questions.detail:
The expansive reading treats the non-refoulement obligation as close to unconditional: a duty this basic, not sending someone back to persecution, cannot be capped by a receiving state’s budget or political mood, so measures that push the line back onto claimants (deterrence, offshore processing, narrow definitions of qualifying danger) shift real risk onto exactly the people the obligation exists to protect.

The limiting reading points out that the modern asylum system routes people through whichever country they successfully reach rather than the one nearest their danger, that a large share of claims are ultimately found not to qualify, and that a state’s capacity to adjudicate fairly and resettle successfully is itself a scarce, finite resource. Treating the obligation as unlimited in practice, on this view, risks either overwhelming the system meant to protect genuine refugees or eroding the public support asylum depends on to survive at all.

questions.text: Over a lifetime and across generations, do immigrants of different skill levels pay in more than they draw out?
questions.why: The verdict swings on accounting choices: an annual snapshot or a lifetime horizon, and whether a migrant’s children count in the ledger.
questions.detail:
The net-positive case stresses long-horizon accounting: even migrants who draw more from schools and services in their early years become working taxpayers for decades afterward, and their children, born and raised in the destination country, pay into the system across their own full working lives. Long-run government fiscal projections built on this kind of multi-generation accounting tend to show the second generation doing much of the heavy lifting that makes the overall lifetime picture favorable.

The net-drain case argues lifetime projections lean on optimistic assumptions about labor-market integration and naturalization that don’t hold for every arrival cohort, and that the annual snapshot, which is what actually strains a given year’s schools, hospitals and benefits budget, looks far worse for lower-skill immigrants and those still early in their settlement. This side also stresses that averaging across all skill levels erases a genuine difference in fiscal outcome between, say, a sponsored skilled worker and someone admitted through a family or humanitarian channel with limited language or credentials.

questions.text: What does immigration do to the wages and employment of the native-born and earlier immigrants who compete most directly with new arrivals?
questions.why: Whether new arrivals complement native workers or substitute for the lowest-wage among them is unsettled labor economics, not politics.
questions.detail:
The complementarity case points to labor markets absorbing supply shocks as capital and firms adjust, natives shifting into higher-skill or language-dependent roles that immigrants are less likely to fill, and economy-wide studies of large historical inflows finding little measurable wage effect on the native-born as a whole, which this side treats as the more reliable read because it covers the full adjustment period rather than a narrow post-shock window.

The substitution case argues that economy-wide averages are exactly the wrong lens: the workers who actually compete with new arrivals are a narrow slice, often earlier immigrants and native workers without a high school diploma, and averaging across the whole labor market can hide real, concentrated wage and job losses at the bottom. This side also notes that the size of any estimated effect depends heavily on an assumption economists cannot directly observe, how substitutable immigrant and native labor really is, which is a modeling choice the field has argued over for decades rather than settled.

questions.text: Can governments actually select the migrants an economy needs, or do points systems and caps reliably misfire?
questions.why: A design question, not one of intent: it turns on whether governments can forecast labor needs, judge foreign credentials, and keep quotas aimed at the occupations actually short of workers.
questions.detail:
Defenders of selective systems point to countries that have run points-based or employer-sponsored admission for decades, adjusting criteria as they go, and argue imperfect selection still beats no selection: even a rough proxy for skill, education, language, or an employer’s job offer in hand, outperforms unmanaged flows at matching admissions to what the labor market actually needs.

Skeptics point to a pattern that recurs across systems that have tried this: selected migrants ending up underemployed relative to their credentials because foreign qualifications go unrecognized, shortage-occupation lists lagging the real labor market by years because government forecasting is unreliable that far out, and caps binding in the wrong sectors entirely. On this reading, a points system’s design on paper says little about whether it delivers the workers an economy actually needs once implemented.

questions.text: Would the very large global income gains projected from freer movement survive the institutional changes that mass movement would bring?
questions.why: The projected gains are modeled with institutions held fixed, and the economist George Borjas argues the scale of movement needed to realize them would itself change those institutions.
questions.detail:
The case that the gains would survive notes the underlying mechanism, a worker becoming far more productive by moving somewhere with better institutions and infrastructure, does not require institutions to stay frozen everywhere at once: large, gradual movements have historically coexisted with receiving-country institutions remaining intact, and partial liberalization well short of instantly open borders could capture much of the projected gain long before any institutional breaking point was tested.

The skeptical case argues the whole projection is a modeling artifact of holding constant the very thing that generates the gain: destination-country institutions are themselves the product of a particular population, culture and political settlement, and admitting people at the scale needed to matter for global poverty is precisely the scenario most likely to change those institutions. Expansionists answer that the objection names no threshold: nothing in the literature identifies the scale at which institutional erosion is supposed to begin, and a liberalization taken in steps can be halted at the first sign that it has.

questions.text: Does a political community have the right to decide its own size and character by limiting who may join?
questions.why: At stake is whether control over membership is self-determination like any other, or a claim over outsiders’ lives that needs more than a preference behind it.
questions.detail:
The self-determination case treats control over membership as inseparable from self-government itself: a community that cannot decide who joins cannot really decide anything else about its own trajectory, from culture to labor markets to the shape of its welfare institutions, and this authority already mirrors how the world treats a state’s control over its own laws and territory as legitimate by default.

The opposing case grants that states govern themselves but denies this extends to a near-unlimited veto over outsiders’ most basic choices about where to live and work: exclusion is coercion exercised against people who never consented to the excluding state’s authority in the first place, and the club or family analogy understates the stakes, weighing a stranger’s whole life chances against existing members’ comparatively modest interest in keeping the door as it is.

questions.text: Does rising diversity from immigration weaken social trust and support for redistribution, or is the link an artifact of other changes?
questions.why: The claim rests on a contested chain from diversity to weakened trust; critics say the correlation really captures poverty, segregation and disinvestment.
questions.detail:
The case for a real effect cites survey evidence that people in more diverse neighborhoods report lower trust and civic engagement, including toward members of their own group, which proponents read as a genuine short-run adjustment cost of a community becoming less homogeneous, one with direct stakes for how generous a public will let its welfare state be toward people it trusts less.

The case that the link is an artifact argues that once income inequality, residential segregation and neighborhood disinvestment are accounted for, the diversity-trust relationship weakens substantially or disappears, and that support for redistribution tracks perceived fiscal fairness and economic insecurity far more than ethnic composition as such. On this reading, diversity is a correlate that shows up because it travels alongside poorer, more unequal neighborhoods, not an independent cause of lower trust.

questions.text: When a rich country recruits doctors and nurses trained by a poor one, is that a fair exchange or a transfer running the wrong way?
questions.why: Skill-selective admission is a decision about someone else’s health system: the same doctor is a gain to one country’s wards and a loss to another’s.
questions.detail:
The fair-exchange case starts with the migrant. A doctor is not her country’s property, and the right to leave is protected by the same rights framework that condemns exclusion, so a policy that keeps her home to serve a national workforce plan is a restriction on her, not on the recruiter. Origin countries also gain in ways a straight loss column misses: remittances to low- and middle-income countries ran at about $685 billion in 2024, more than foreign direct investment and official development assistance combined; returning migrants bring back training and capital; and the prospect of emigrating is argued to raise the number of people who enter training at all, so a country can finish with more health workers at home rather than fewer.

The case that the transfer runs the wrong way points at who paid for the training. A poor state that funded a medical education out of a thin public budget loses the money and the ward the graduate would have staffed, and remittances arrive as private income to a household, not as staff in a clinic. That is the reasoning behind the WHO Global Code of Practice and its safeguards list of 55 countries whose health workforce is thin enough that WHO discourages active recruitment from them outright: on this reading some of these flows are not a market at all but a subsidy running from the poorest health systems to the richest, and the destination state, not the migrant, is the party choosing to draw on it.

positions.name: Border Sovereigntist
positions.steelman: A nation that cannot control its own border has stopped being self-governing.
positions.description: Democratic self-government begins at the border: a political community that cannot decide who joins it has already lost the most basic power a sovereign people holds. Citizenship is membership in a bounded project of self-rule, not a service contract, and that project cannot survive an entry system the state does not actually control. US Customs and Border Protection recorded more than 2.4 million migrant encounters at the southern border in fiscal year 2023 alone, a scale no enforcement system was ever built to process. Admissions should be set by the public through its elected government, not by whoever manages to cross first, and the numbers should come down until enforcement matches the law on the books.
positions.detail:
Michael Walzer’s Spheres of Justice (1983) supplied the philosophical anchor decades before border sovereignty became a mainstream political fight: a political community’s right to admit or exclude members is inseparable from its right to run its own internal life. Yoram Hazony’s The Virtue of Nationalism (2018) restated the case for a newly hostile era, arguing the bounded nation-state, not empire or open borders, is what actually protects self-determination and cultural pluralism among peoples. On the operational side, the Center for Immigration Studies (Mark Krikorian) and NumbersUSA (Roy Beck) have spent three decades pushing Washington toward one concrete goal: bring legal admissions and enforcement capacity back into alignment, the logic behind proposals like Senator Tom Cotton’s RAISE Act to cut legal immigration toward its historical average.

The camp splits on sequencing: hardliners want the border demonstrably controlled and numbers down before any expanded legal channel reopens, while a more pragmatic wing, closer to the Skills Selector position, would trade tighter enforcement now for a modernized, selective system later. What holds the position together against the charge of simple xenophobia is the Walzerian point that every functioning democracy already restricts membership somehow, so the live question was never whether to control entry, only who gets to decide it, the citizenry through its government, or whoever crosses first.

The other half of the case is not procedural at all, and this camp’s own writers state it plainly: how many people a country admits in future is a legitimate object of democratic choice, not merely a residual of what an enforcement system can process. Hazony’s nation-state exists so that a people can keep its own way of life and hand it on, which makes the size and composition of future intakes exactly the sort of question a self-governing public is entitled to settle for itself. Douglas Murray’s The Strange Death of Europe (2017) presses the sharper European version: postwar admissions ran at a scale and pace no electorate was ever asked to approve, and a political community that has lost the confidence to say what it is has no ground left on which to say who may join it. That is where this camp’s ceiling parts from the Skills Selector’s, which sets the number by what a labor market can absorb. The claim now travels on party platforms as well as in books: Reform UK campaigns on freezing all non-essential immigration while keeping a narrow route for the skills it calls essential.
positions.proponents: Mark Krikorian (Center for Immigration Studies), Roy Beck (NumbersUSA), Yoram Hazony, Douglas Murray, Sen. Tom Cotton, Viktor Orbán
positions.representative_note: Three-decade Washington think tank arguing immigration levels should be set by what the state can actually enforce and the public will accept, not by who arrives first.

positions.name: Skills Selector
positions.steelman: Immigration is policy: admit the skills and numbers the economy needs.
positions.description: Immigration policy should work like any other lever of economic management, matched deliberately to what the labor market and public services can absorb, rather than left to family chains, a visa lottery or an open-ended asylum queue. The RAISE Act, the 2017 Cotton-Perdue proposal, showed the shape: a points test scoring age, English fluency, education and salary, with the highest marks for STEM doctorates and job offers paying triple the state median wage. Canada already runs a working version in Express Entry, which ranks applicants on the same criteria and invites candidates from the top of the list, while Australia runs its own points-tested skilled program and the UK ties eligibility to salary thresholds and a time-limited shortage list. None of this requires shutting the door: legal, capped, skills-weighted channels are how a country keeps immigration politically sustainable, because it can point to exactly who was let in and why.
positions.detail:
Canada pioneered the point system in 1967, replacing an explicitly race-based admissions test with one scored on education, age and language; Australia dropped the last of the White Australia rules in 1973 and adopted its own points-based selection, NUMAS, in 1979. The US debate over importing that model runs back decades but crystallized in the 2017 RAISE Act, the Cotton-Perdue bill that would have cut family-sponsored “chain” categories and much of the diversity lottery in favor of a test scoring age, English fluency, education and salary, with the top marks reserved for STEM doctorates and job offers paying triple the state median wage. It never passed, but reform proposals since keep returning to the same architecture.

Both Canada and Australia’s own numbers forced a revision of the doctrine. A pure point system, scoring credentials and language in isolation, produced immigrant employment rates measurably below the native-born, because a strong test score doesn’t guarantee a matching job on arrival. Both countries responded by weighting the system toward employer- and labor-market-tied criteria, and both keep revising: Canada awarded bonus points for a validated Canadian job offer until March 2025, when it withdrew them to curb abuse of the labor-market-impact process, while keeping the category-based Express Entry draws aimed at named occupations and the provincial nominee streams that do the same work. The UK has been narrowing rather than extending its shortage route: the Shortage Occupation List was abolished in April 2024, and the Temporary Shortage List introduced from July 2025 is time-limited and confined to below-degree-level occupations the Migration Advisory Committee judges crucial to the industrial strategy or to critical infrastructure. The lesson this camp draws isn’t that selection failed; it’s that selection has to track the labor market in real time, not a static credential scorecard.

The case doesn’t rest on any single study; it rests on convergence. Canada, Australia, the UK and the plan the US came closest to enacting in 2017 arrived at the same core design under different politics: age, language and education first, then employer or labor-market validation layered on top. That four independent systems kept re-deriving the same answer is the strongest evidence this camp has that selecting for tested skills and demonstrated labor-market fit beats an unmanaged lottery or an open-ended family and asylum queue, for the immigrant and the receiving country alike.
positions.proponents: George Borjas, Tom Cotton and David Perdue (RAISE Act), the UK Migration Advisory Committee, Brian Bell, Canada’s Express Entry / IRCC
positions.representative_note: Ranks applicants by age, education, language and work experience, then invites the top of the list — the model most skills-based reform proposals point to.

positions.name: Cohesion Communitarian
positions.steelman: A welfare state runs on trust between strangers: build that slowly, or watch it drain.
positions.description: A generous welfare state and a society where strangers extend each other trust are the same achievement, built through shared schools, workplaces and civic life over time, not granted automatically to whoever arrives next. Robert Putnam’s study of American communities found that, in the near term, greater ethnic diversity tracked with lower trust among neighbors of every background. A parallel pattern appears in public spending: ethnically fragmented localities have been found to devote a smaller share of it to the shared goods that redistribution depends on. The conclusion is not a closed door but a pace, with integration support, that lets newcomers become fellow citizens.
positions.detail:
Putnam did not set out to hand ammunition to restrictionists: he is a lifelong liberal, and his 2007 paper closed by insisting that immigration remains a net positive and that new, more encompassing identities can be built over time. But the immediate finding held up under scrutiny; across a sample running from Los Angeles to rural South Dakota, people in more diverse communities trusted neighbors, local government, and even close friends less, and the pattern survived controls for income, crime and length of residence. What communitarians take from it is not Putnam’s policy conclusion but his mechanism: trust between strangers is a produced good, made through repeated contact inside shared institutions, and a community given too little time to make it will simply have less of it.

David Goodhart gave the argument its sharpest formulation in a 2004 essay that asked ‘Too Diverse?’: a large, redistributive welfare state is an expensive act of solidarity between strangers, and that solidarity has historically been easiest to sustain inside a population that already feels like one people, so a country pushing hard on both diversity and redistribution at once puts the second at risk. Economists Alberto Alesina, Reza Baqir and William Easterly found a matching signature in the data: American localities with more ethnic fragmentation spent markedly less on the public goods (schools, roads, sewers) that collective welfare requires. Sweden’s retreat after 2015 from one of Europe’s most open asylum policies, under strain on housing, schools and public trust in its own generous system, is the case this camp points to when asked what the trade-off looks like once it stops being theoretical.

Where this position breaks from outright restrictionism is on what follows from the diagnosis, not on whether numbers are anyone’s business. Miller defends a democracy’s right to cap numbers and to weigh cultural and demographic continuity, and denies that capping them is unjust; Goodhart argues numbers should come down to a level integration can absorb, and that integration itself must be funded rather than assumed. What separates both from restrictionism is the aim: a pace and scale a society’s integrating institutions can actually carry, not the smallest possible number. Paul Collier’s Exodus pushes the same logic into economics: it is the rate of diaspora growth and the strength of integration policy, not migrant numbers on their own, that decide whether a given inflow builds a society’s social capital or drains it. Reihan Salam’s case for a smaller, more assimilation-focused American immigration policy carries the same argument into a country with no European-style welfare state to defend, which exposes the position’s live fault line: whether what is being protected is the redistributive state, the interpersonal trust that any free society needs to function, or both together.
positions.proponents: David Miller, David Goodhart, Paul Collier, Reihan Salam
positions.representative_note: Journalist and Policy Exchange think-tank director whose 2004 essay ‘Too Diverse?’ named the diversity-solidarity trade-off that anchors this position.

positions.name: Economic Expansionist
positions.steelman: An aging economy grows one way: more workers, more taxpayers, more ideas.
positions.description: A modern economy’s growth is arithmetic: more workers, more taxpayers, more people inventing things, and native fertility has fallen below replacement across the rich world. The Congressional Budget Office found the 2021–2026 immigration surge would add about $8.9 trillion to GDP and cut federal deficits by roughly $0.9 trillion over 2024 to 2034. Immigrants founded or cofounded 455 of America’s 775 billion-dollar startups, and the National Academies of Sciences finds second-generation immigrants are among the strongest fiscal contributors in the country. None of this is a case for open borders: it is a case for setting legal immigration high enough to keep the workforce and the tax base growing.
positions.detail:
This case took its current shape as the demographic math got harder to ignore: the baby boom aged into retirement just as native fertility fell below the replacement rate of 2.1, a trend now standard across the rich world. The Immigration Act of 1990, which expanded employment-based visas, and the tech industry’s long push on H-1B caps were early skirmishes; the National Academies of Sciences’ 2016 report, The Economic and Fiscal Consequences of Immigration, became the reference text once Congress needed a nonpartisan answer to “does this pay for itself.” Advocates increasingly point across the Pacific and Atlantic: Japan, South Korea and Italy show what a rich economy looks like when it lets the workforce shrink instead of using the immigration release valve.

The camp splits over how selective the pipeline needs to be. One wing, closer to a pure points-based system, wants growth-boosting immigration to be mostly high-skill; the broader wing argues the payoff shows up a generation later regardless of entry skill level, since the National Academies found first-generation immigrants cost more in services than they pay in taxes but their children are among the strongest fiscal contributors in the country. On wages, expansionists treat the long-running Card–Borjas dispute as settled in their favor: David Card’s natural-experiment studies, starting with the Mariel boatlift, found no material wage damage to native workers overall, which is why this camp treats restrictionist wage fears as a distributional problem to manage at the margin, not a reason to cap the total.

The single number this camp reaches for most is the CBO’s: a projected $8.9 trillion of extra GDP and roughly $0.9 trillion of deficit reduction over 2024 to 2034 from the 2021–2026 immigration surge alone, delivered with no legislative change, purely through more people working and paying tax. On innovation, the National Foundation for American Policy’s count of immigrant founders or cofounders behind 455 of America’s 775 billion-dollar startups gets cited constantly as proof the payoff isn’t just fiscal arithmetic. Canada and Australia, which run explicit high-immigration growth strategies through points systems, are held up as the policy executed well.
positions.proponents: Giovanni Peri, Madeline Zavodny, Fwd.us, New American Economy, Cato Institute, National Academies of Sciences (2016 report)
positions.representative_note: UC Davis economist and director of its Global Migration Center, whose research on immigrant inflows raising native productivity and wages underpins the mainstream growth case.

positions.name: Asylum Rights Defender
positions.steelman: Persecution triggers a legal duty to protect, not a number a government can set.
positions.description: Asylum is not immigration policy by another name: it is the legal duty a state owes anyone within its reach who faces persecution for who they are or what they believe, fixed by the 1951 Refugee Convention and, through non-refoulement, binding even on states that never signed it. That duty cannot be capped, auctioned, or weighed against a skills quota, because a claim turns on the danger a person faces, not on how many admission slots are left for the year. UNHCR counted 117.8 million people forcibly displaced at the end of 2025, while global resettlement placements have run at a small fraction of its own assessed need. Refusing to hear a persecution claim, or returning someone to the danger they fled, is not a control choice but a breach of a standing legal obligation.
positions.detail:
The 1951 Refugee Convention was written by people who had just watched states turn persecution into someone else’s problem: in 1939 Cuba, then the United States, then Canada each refused to land the more than 900 Jewish passengers of the MS St. Louis, and the ship sailed back to Europe, where 254 of them were later killed in the Holocaust. The Convention’s core promise, non-refoulement, was drawn precisely to close that door for good. The 1967 Protocol then stripped away the original European and pre-1951 limits, turning a regional postwar fix into a standing, open-ended obligation, which is exactly why this camp treats it as categorically different from a visa program that a legislature can resize each year.

The legal theory behind that distinction, most fully worked out by James Hathaway, is that refugee status is surrogate protection: a substitute for the protection a person’s own state has failed or refused to provide, triggered by that person’s circumstances rather than granted at a government’s discretion the way a work permit is. Courts have enforced the duty against states that tried to engineer around it. In Hirsi Jamaa and Others v. Italy (2012), the European Court of Human Rights held that intercepting migrants at sea and returning them to Libya breached non-refoulement even though it happened outside Italian territory, because the obligation travels with state agents, not with a line on a map.

The camp is not united on how far enforcement should reach. Pragmatists, UNHCR and resettlement agencies such as the International Rescue Committee among them, back the 2018 Global Compact on Refugees and reformed burden sharing between rich and poor host states, treating orderly resettlement as a necessary supplement to the duty rather than a threat to it. Hathaway marks the camp’s other wing: surrogate protection as the legal theory, plus binding, negotiated responsibility-sharing between rich and poor host states, with the Compact criticized from inside the camp, in his 2018 phrase a ‘cop-out’, as too weak to deliver it. Rights groups such as Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch take a harder line, opposing offshoring arrangements like the UK’s abandoned Rwanda scheme on the ground that a wealthy state cannot contract out a legal duty it owes in its own jurisdiction to a poorer transit country. Both wings agree on the point that matters most to the wider debate: the obligation itself is not something a quota, a deterrent policy, or a bilateral deal can extinguish.
positions.proponents: James Hathaway, Guy S. Goodwin-Gill, UNHCR, Human Rights First, International Rescue Committee, Amnesty International
positions.representative_note: The UN agency mandated to supervise the 1951 Convention; its Global Trends data anchors this camp’s case for the scale of the obligation.

positions.name: Membership by Presence
positions.steelman: Ten years of life in a place makes you a member; the law is only late in saying so.
positions.description: A person who has lived, worked and raised a family in a place for a decade is already a member of that society; what is missing is the paper, not the belonging. Time and ties, not the manner of entry, are what make someone part of a community, which is why removing a long-settled neighbor does not restore a rule broken years ago: it destroys the life built since. Joseph Carens makes the case in The Ethics of Immigration: grant a state wide discretion over whom to admit, and it still follows from ordinary liberal democratic norms that anyone resident for several years, with or without authorization, has a moral claim to the status and rights of citizenship. Family unity rests on the same premise, which is why a spouse or a child belongs here as the relationship the claim is made of, not as a visa category to be traded away in a reform package.
positions.detail:
Carens built the argument to survive a reader who rejects open borders. The Ethics of Immigration (2013) grants, for the sake of the argument, that a state may exercise considerable discretionary control over admission, then asks what follows once a person is inside. Social membership, on his account, is distinct from legal citizenship: someone becomes a member of a society by residing in it for an extended period and forming an identity, interests and personal attachments there. The claim that membership generates grows with elapsed time and past some point outweighs the state’s interest in enforcing the admission rule that was broken to create it. That is the philosophical basis for an amnesty, and it is deliberately independent of the birthplace-arbitrariness case Carens is better known for, which is why proponents who want nothing to do with open borders can hold this position without inconsistency.

Linda Bosniak’s The Citizen and the Alien (2006) works the same ground from constitutional law rather than moral philosophy, asking what rights aliens residing inside a liberal democracy do and should enjoy while remaining outside political citizenship, and naming the unease between a polity that polices its edge hard and one that extends near-equal treatment to those already within it. Elizabeth F. Cohen’s The Political Value of Time (2018) supplies the practical version: liberal democracies already convert measured duration into rights, through residency clocks, waiting periods and cut-off dates that decide who counts as in. The camp’s point is that this currency is already in circulation and simply spent inconsistently, generously on those who entered through one door and not at all on those who entered through another.

The movement voices carry it into policy. The National Immigration Law Center fights for a path to citizenship and backs bills that would repeal the three- and ten-year unlawful-presence bars keeping long-resident people from adjusting status through a spouse or parent; United We Dream, which describes itself as built and powered by immigrant youth, organizes the constituency with the longest residence and the weakest claim on paper; UnidosUS presses the same case in mainstream advocacy. The internal split is over the endpoint: a full path to citizenship, or a secure permanent status short of naturalization that ends deportability without settling the political question. Against the sovereigntist the line is not that the rule never mattered but that its remedy has expired: enforcement against someone rooted for a decade does not restore the border as it stood, it removes a neighbor, a coworker and often a parent. The objection this camp has to answer is precedent, that legalizing one cohort teaches the next that presence eventually converts to status, which is the reading restrictionists give the 1986 Immigration Reform and Control Act. The answer offered is that the alternative is not fewer arrivals but a permanent resident population with no standing, and that a settled class of people the law refuses to see does more damage to the authority of law than recognizing what is already the case.
positions.proponents: Joseph Carens, Linda Bosniak, Elizabeth F. Cohen, National Immigration Law Center, United We Dream, UnidosUS
positions.representative_note: His The Ethics of Immigration (2013) makes the social-membership case: residence and elapsed time, not the manner of entry, generate a moral claim to membership, an argument built to hold even for readers who grant the state wide control over admission.

positions.name: Family Unity Advocate
positions.steelman: A spouse or a child is a reason of its own, not a category to trade away.
positions.description: A family is not a labor-market input, and keeping one together is a reason for admission in its own right, not a legacy category to be traded away for points. It is also how most legal immigration actually happens: of the 1,364,090 people who became lawful permanent residents of the United States in fiscal 2024, about 63% qualified through a family relationship. Calling that a chain misdescribes the statute, which lets a citizen petition only for a spouse, a child, a parent or a sibling, and creates no category at all for a cousin, an aunt or a grandparent. The ask is not an open door: it is recapturing visas Congress authorized and never issued, lifting the per-country ceilings, and ending a wait that close to four million people with approved petitions are serving abroad.
positions.detail:
The claim is older than any national immigration statute. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights calls the family “the natural and fundamental group unit of society” and entitled to protection by society and the state, language repeated in Article 23 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights turns respect for family life into something courts enforce, and the European Union’s 2003 Family Reunification Directive makes reunification an entitlement, subject to conditions, for lawfully resident third-country nationals rather than a favor. What this camp draws from that sequence is that family unity is protected in the same instruments that ground the rest of rights law, so it is not a concession an admissions system extends when it happens to have spare capacity.

In the United States the organizing vehicle is the Value Our Families coalition, which describes its work as advocating for policies that make the family immigration system fairer, more efficient, and more effective. Asian Americans Advancing Justice - AAJC, whose president and executive director John C. Yang has been among the case’s most visible voices, the National Immigration Forum, UnidosUS and the American Immigration Council press the same argument. Its current legislative vehicle is the Reuniting Families Act of 2025, introduced by Representative Judy Chu and Senator Mazie Hirono as H.R. 6565 and S. 3419 and endorsed by more than fifty organizations, which would recapture unused visas from earlier years, raise the per-country ceilings, exempt the spouses and minor children of permanent residents from the numerical caps, and set an outer limit on how long a family can be made to wait. The bill this camp defines itself against is the RAISE Act, which would have abolished the sibling and adult-children categories outright and replaced permanent admission of a citizen’s parents with a renewable five-year visa carrying no work authorization and no access to public benefits.

Against the argument that these visas should be converted into points, the reply comes in two parts. The first refuses the premise: a spouse or a child is not an economic input whose entry has to clear a wage percentile, and a country that tells a citizen her mother may come only if the mother scores well has changed what that citizenship is worth. The second meets selection on its own ground. Harriet Duleep and Mark Regets find that immigrants admitted outside occupational categories, most of them family migrants, start with lower earnings than employment-selected immigrants but see earnings grow faster, catching up after roughly eleven to eighteen years, because people not admitted for a job already in hand invest more heavily in new skills once they arrive. The National Academies’ 2016 synthesis supplies the generational version: the US-born children of immigrants are among the strongest net fiscal contributors of any group in the country, and a family visa is how many of those children come to be born there. Selection systems lean on family admission whether they say so or not, since skilled workers arrive with spouses and children and rich countries compete for them partly on whether the family can come at all.

The European front is about suspension rather than replacement. Germany’s Act on the Suspension of Family Reunification for Beneficiaries of Subsidiary Protection took effect on 24 July 2025 and closes that route for two years, to 23 July 2027, on the stated ground of relieving pressure on admission and integration systems; the International Refugee Assistance Project and German legal scholars argue it cannot be squared with Article 8 of the Convention. The camp’s own split is over ambition. One wing wants the backlog cleared and little else: recapture the unissued visas, lift the country caps, and the structure Congress built in 1965 does what it was meant to do. The other holds that the categories themselves are drawn too narrowly for how families are actually composed, and would add permanent partners, stepchildren and adoptees rather than only speed up a queue for the relatives already on the list.
positions.proponents: Value Our Families coalition, Asian Americans Advancing Justice - AAJC (John C. Yang), National Immigration Forum, American Immigration Council, UnidosUS, Rep. Judy Chu and Sen. Mazie Hirono (Reuniting Families Act)
positions.representative_note: Coalition of national and local organizations campaigning to protect and expand family immigration; its current vehicle, the Reuniting Families Act, would recapture unused visas, lift per-country ceilings and cap how long a family can be made to wait.

positions.name: Wage Protectionist
positions.steelman: Flood the supply of workers and the price of labor falls: economics, not nativism.
positions.description: Labor is a market like any other: flood the supply of people competing for the same jobs and the price of that labor, the wage, falls, hardest on workers with the fewest other options. George Borjas’s simulation of the 1980–2000 immigration wave, which raised the supply of working men by 11 percent, put the short-run wage loss at 8.9 percent for native workers without a high school diploma, against 3.2 percent for the average native worker. Letting capital adjust shrinks those figures unevenly: in his 1990 to 2010 simulation the long-run effect on the average native worker washes out to zero while workers without a high school diploma are still down 3.1 percent. This is a claim about numbers bidding for the same jobs, not about who those people are, so the fix is a labor-market lever: slower, more selective inflows, and a wage floor defended for earlier immigrants too.
positions.detail:
This argument has a labor, not a nationalist, pedigree. Samuel Gompers built the American Federation of Labor partly on a platform of restricting immigration to protect wage rates, and the same logic ran through the United Farm Workers’ early opposition to undocumented labor undercutting farmworker strikes. Bernie Sanders revived the framing in 2015, telling an interviewer that open borders was “a right-wing proposal” that would flood the country with cheap labor and gut wages for Americans already struggling, a line that drew as much fire from the left as from immigration advocates.

The evidentiary fight centers on the 1980 Mariel boatlift, when roughly 125,000 Cuban refugees arrived in Miami within months. David Card’s 1990 study found no measurable wage effect on Miami’s low-skilled workers and became the standard reference for the view that local labor markets absorb even large, sudden inflows. Borjas’s 2017 reanalysis, narrowing the comparison group to non-Hispanic male workers without a high school diploma, found wages for that group fell sharply relative to similar cities, a result Giovanni Peri, Vasil Yasenov, and others have contested on grounds of sample size and comparison-city choice. The dispute has never fully settled, which this camp reads as reason for caution rather than as vindication for the other side.

The 2016 National Academies of Sciences report, often cited against this position for finding small wage effects overall, is read here as confirming the mechanism rather than refuting it: the report itself concentrates the measurable wage loss on native workers without a high school diploma and on earlier immigrants, exactly the groups competing most directly with new arrivals. That concentration, not the economy-wide average, is what a labor policy is supposed to protect against.
positions.proponents: George Borjas, Vernon M. Briggs Jr., Steven Camarota, Center for Immigration Studies, Samuel Gompers, Bernie Sanders
positions.representative_note: Harvard economist whose factor-proportions studies and Mariel boatlift reanalysis are this camp’s empirical backbone.

positions.name: Origin-Country Advocate
positions.steelman: Recruiting a poor country’s scarce doctors is aid running backwards.
positions.description: Every skilled migrant a rich country selects was trained somewhere, usually at someone else’s public expense, and the country that paid keeps the bill and loses the ward. That is why the World Health Assembly adopted the Global Code of Practice on the International Recruitment of Health Personnel in 2010, and why WHO publishes a safeguards list, 55 countries in its 2023 edition, whose health workforce is thin enough that it discourages active recruitment from them. Remittances are real money, about $685 billion to low- and middle-income countries in 2024, but a household transfer does not staff a clinic that has lost its only surgeon. The ask is not that borders close: it is that a destination state treat its own selection criteria as a policy with consequences elsewhere.
positions.detail:
The institutional anchor is the WHO Global Code of Practice on the International Recruitment of Health Personnel, adopted by the 63rd World Health Assembly on 21 May 2010 as resolution WHA63.16. It is voluntary, which this camp treats as a point of leverage rather than a defeat: it establishes that recruiting actively out of a country in workforce crisis is something a government can be asked to answer for. Article 5 is where it bites, and the WHO health workforce support and safeguards list is how it is operationalized. The 2023 edition names 55 countries, 37 of them in the African region, whose universal-health-coverage service index and health-worker density both fall below the thresholds WHO sets, and WHO discourages active recruitment from them by public and private sector employers and recruiters alike. On 29 May 2026 the 79th World Health Assembly amended the Code, extending it to health personnel recruited internationally as care workers, applying its recommendations during health emergencies, and encouraging co-investment in health systems and the health workforce so that international recruitment returns proportional benefit to source as well as destination countries; WHO says an updated safeguards list follows later in 2026, with added flexibility for listed countries to signal a willingness to allow active recruitment and for unlisted states to request support. The camp reads the co-investment language as its own remedy, restraint paired with support, finally written into the instrument rather than only argued for.

The scholarly case runs alongside it. Devesh Kapur and John McHale’s Give Us Your Best and Brightest weighed the channels through which skilled emigration reaches a sending country, remittances, return, diaspora networks and the incentive to train, against the loss of the people themselves, and concluded that the global hunt for talent is not costless for the countries losing the talent. Gillian Brock and Michael Blake’s Debating Brain Drain pushes the harder question of what, if anything, a poor state may demand of the citizens it educated. Most of this camp declines to follow that argument as far as exit restrictions: the leverage it wants sits on the recruiting end, where the choice is being made by a wealthy government that could choose otherwise.

Where it breaks with skills-based selection is over what a selection criterion actually is. A points test that rewards a medical degree is not a neutral instrument for reading the destination labor market; it is a standing offer aimed at exactly the professions the poorest health systems cannot replace, and the migrant who answers it is not the one who should have to weigh the cost. The remedy the Code pairs with restraint is support: the same list that limits active recruitment marks those countries as needing priority investment in health workforce development and health system strengthening, on the view that fencing a shortage off without funding a way out of it only freezes the shortage in place.
positions.proponents: World Health Organization (Global Code of Practice, 2010), Devesh Kapur and John McHale, Gillian Brock, Michael Blake
positions.representative_note: Adopted by the World Health Assembly in 2010; the safeguards list built on its Article 5 names 55 countries, as of 2023, from which WHO discourages active recruitment of health workers.

positions.name: Migrant Labor Rights Defender
positions.steelman: A worker who cannot quit has no wage floor.
positions.description: Every labor protection on the books runs on one thing: the worker’s ability to walk away. Tie legal status to the employer who sponsored it and that exit disappears, so wage theft, seized documents, debts from illegal recruitment fees and retaliation are not bad apples but what the visa design predicts. Centro de los Derechos del Migrante’s Ripe for Reform, built on interviews with 100 H-2A workers, documents discrimination, sexual harassment, wage theft and health and safety violations running through that program. The remedy is neither a lower cap nor a bigger temporary program: it is authorization the worker carries, portable across employers, with enforceable contracts, no recruitment fees charged to workers, union access and protection for anyone who complains.
positions.detail:
The diagnosis is structural rather than moral. Most temporary work visas bind a worker’s legal presence to a single sponsoring employer, so the threat of dismissal is also a threat of removal, and the ordinary remedy for a bad job, leaving it for a better one, is unavailable. Daniel Costa of the Economic Policy Institute puts the mechanism plainly for the H-2B program: because the visa is employer-sponsored, guestworkers cannot switch jobs if they are exploited or robbed of wages. Recruitment debt tightens the same screw from the other end, since a worker who paid fees to get the job cannot afford to lose it. On this account abuse is not a failure to enforce the rules but a predictable consequence of the rule that ties status to a sponsor, which is why this camp treats visa-condition design, rather than enforcement funding, as the thing to change.

The vehicle is a coalition rather than a single author. The International Labor Recruitment Working Group, founded in 2011 and now operating as Migration that Works, brought labor, migration, civil rights and anti-trafficking organizations together to work across visa categories instead of one program at a time; its members include the AFL-CIO, SEIU, UNITE HERE, the Economic Policy Institute, the Southern Poverty Law Center, Farmworker Justice, the National Employment Law Project, the National Domestic Workers Alliance, the National Immigration Law Center and Centro de los Derechos del Migrante, and it covers the H-2A, H-2B, H-1B, J-1 and TN categories together. That breadth is part of the argument: the same structural complaint is made about a farmworker in Georgia and a software engineer on an H-1B, because in both cases the sponsor holds the status.

The camp splits over whether a sponsored temporary program can be repaired at all. One wing wants portability, enforceable contracts, recruitment-fee bans, union access and whistleblower protection written into the visas that exist; another argues that a labor need recurring every year should be met by admitting permanent residents who can quit, and that no set of conditions rescues a status designed to expire. Both wings reject the two remedies their neighbors offer. Against wage protectionism they hold that cutting the number of visas leaves the workers who remain exactly as unable to quit as before, and that a workforce which can be silenced is itself what drags the wage floor down for everyone. Against the mobility-partnership case they hold that more temporary permits, on the terms these programs are written, expands the mechanism rather than the opportunity.
positions.proponents: AFL-CIO, Economic Policy Institute (Daniel Costa), Southern Poverty Law Center, Farmworker Justice, Centro de los Derechos del Migrante, Migration that Works (formerly the International Labor Recruitment Working Group)
positions.representative_note: Coalition of labor, migration, civil rights and anti-trafficking organizations, founded in 2011 as the International Labor Recruitment Working Group, pressing for worker protections across the H-2A, H-2B, H-1B, J-1 and TN visa categories at once.

positions.name: Mobility Partnership Pragmatist
positions.steelman: Let people work abroad without waiting on a passport: that is where the gains are.
positions.description: The fight over permanent settlement is the wrong fight: the largest gain from migration is collected the day someone starts work abroad, not the day they naturalize, since a worker of identical age, education and skill earns several times more simply by moving from a poor country to a rich one. The instrument is therefore the negotiated deal rather than the open border or the points test: rationed, renewable work permits agreed country to country, with training run in the origin country so it ends up with more skilled workers rather than fewer. Italy has authorized 497,550 work permits for 2026 to 2028, with quotas reserved for countries that sign cooperation agreements and training moved upstream into them. That is what this argument looks like once it stops being a book.
positions.detail:
Lant Pritchett set out the diagnosis in Let Their People Come (Center for Global Development, 2006): irresistible demographic pressure for labor mobility running into immovable rich-country ideas about who may settle, a deadlock that will not be argued away. His answer was six accommodations designed to be politically acceptable rather than philosophically pure, among them far greater use of temporary work permits, explicit rationing of their number, and bilateral rather than multilateral agreements. Michael Clemens supplies the size of the prize with the place premium, the several-fold wage gap between identical workers in poor and rich countries. Both men are routinely filed with the open-borders camp and both decline the label: openborders.info’s own page on Clemens records that he does not support complete open borders while favoring substantially freer migration, and Pritchett’s accommodations are offered precisely as the alternative to free movement.

The position now has institutions rather than only authors. The Center for Global Development runs the research program; Labor Mobility Partnerships states its purpose as creating better job opportunities for half a billion workers from low-income countries by 2050, through demonstration projects in specific corridors, technical assistance to governments and industry, and coalition-building toward pathways it calls reliable, rights-respecting and financially sustainable. The Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration, adopted by 164 states in December 2018, wrote the mechanism into its Objective 18, which encourages global skills partnerships that build training capacity in origin countries and prepare trainees for employability in the labor markets of every participating country. Italy is the working example at scale: its 2026 to 2028 flow decree authorizes 497,550 work permits, reserves quotas for countries holding cooperation agreements with it, among them Algeria, India, Morocco, Senegal, Sri Lanka, Peru, Tunisia and Ukraine, and pushes training into the countries people leave from.

The camp is not a softer version of its neighbors, and says so. It does not argue from a right to move, and it accepts numerical control, which is what separates it from open borders. It parts from skills-based selection on the object: selecting people for temporary work rather than for permanent membership, and co-financing their training abroad instead of harvesting credentials already paid for elsewhere. And it parts from origin-country advocacy on direction, wanting recruitment restructured so the sending country gains rather than restrained so it loses less. Two objections press from opposite flanks. Migrant labor rights defenders argue that a permit tied to a single sponsor removes the worker’s power to quit, which is the lever every other protection depends on; the answer here is that portability, enforceable contracts and repeat access are exactly the standard this camp’s own institutions have set for the permits they design, so the objection specifies how the instrument must be built rather than making a case against it. From the other flank comes the charge that work without a path to membership manufactures a class of people with jobs and no standing; the answer there is that the realistic alternative on offer is not membership but exclusion.
positions.proponents: Lant Pritchett, Michael Clemens, Center for Global Development, Labor Mobility Partnerships (LaMP), Global Compact for Migration (Objective 18)
positions.representative_note: Development economist whose Let Their People Come (Center for Global Development, 2006) proposed rationed temporary permits and bilateral agreements as the politically acceptable route to far more labor mobility.

positions.name: Open Borders Universalist
positions.steelman: Birthplace is luck, not merit; fencing a willing worker out costs the world trillions.
positions.description: Where a person is born is luck, not merit, and luck confers no right to fence anyone out of a job, a home, or a life a peaceful stranger is willing to build. Turning away a willing worker and a willing employer is not neutral border management; it is the state using force to block a voluntary exchange. Michael Clemens’s survey in the Journal of Economic Perspectives found that erasing migration barriers worldwide could raise global output by 50 to 150 percent, trillion-dollar bills left lying on the sidewalk. The same worker earns several times more for identical work the moment he crosses into a rich country, so free movement should be the default and every restriction should have to earn its keep.
positions.detail:
Joseph Carens set the modern terms in 1987, comparing citizenship by birth to feudal privilege: an inherited, unchosen status that decides most of a person’s life chances before she has done anything to earn or lose them. Reasoning from behind a Rawlsian veil of ignorance, he argued that no one designing a fair world without knowing where they would be born would hand one lucky group a permanent veto over who else may join them.

The camp splits more on foundations than on conclusions. Huemer argues from individual rights: blocking a willing worker and a willing employer from trading is coercion against both, no different in kind from a government stopping a sale between two of its own citizens, and demands the same overriding-harm justification any use of force does. Caplan and economists such as John Kennan build the case from welfare economics instead, treating exclusion as an unpriced tax on the world’s poor. The two threads mostly converge on tactics: Caplan’s ‘keyhole solutions’ (admission taxes, temporary work permits, surtaxes, delayed welfare eligibility) aim to neutralize the wage, fiscal and cohesion objections without abandoning the open-borders default, a compromise some purists in the movement see as conceding ground the argument does not need to give up.

A separate thread arrives at the same door from the left and rejects the market framing that gets it there. Harsha Walia’s Border and Rule argues that a border is not a neutral filter but a mechanism of labor segmentation and racial ordering: it manufactures a workforce that can be worked without rights and removed when surplus, which makes the problem not foreign workers but the sorting itself. Displacement, on this account, is the outcome of conquest, capitalist globalization and climate breakdown, so the states policing the border are implicated in the movement they police. What follows is border abolition and migrant justice rather than a better-priced admission scheme, which is why this wing rejects the keyhole compromises and the desirable-versus-undesirable sorting that skills-based selection is built on as readily as it rejects exclusion itself.

The evidentiary anchor on the economic side is the place premium: Clemens, Montenegro and Pritchett found that a worker of identical age, education and skill earns several times more simply by relocating from a poor country to a rich one, a gap far larger than any measurable difference in productivity. Clemens’s 2011 review in the Journal of Economic Perspectives, ‘Economics and Emigration: Trillion-Dollar Bills on the Sidewalk?’, put the potential gain from removing migration barriers worldwide at 50 to 150 percent of global output, dwarfing the gains from finishing the job on trade and capital liberalization.
positions.proponents: Bryan Caplan, Michael Huemer, Joseph Carens, Alex Tabarrok, John Kennan, Harsha Walia, No One Is Illegal
positions.representative_note: ‘Open Borders: The Science and Ethics of Immigration’ (2019, with artist Zach Weinersmith) is the fullest single statement of the case, splicing the economic evidence with the moral argument in one accessible book.

crux.lead: Beneath the numbers fight lies a prior question: whose claim the border must answer.
crux.lead_highlight: whose claim the border must answer
crux.subtitle: Each camp names a different claimant: a self-governing polity, an aging economy, the person in danger, the low-wage worker, the settled neighbor the law still calls a stranger, the spouse or child waiting out a queue on the other side, anyone born elsewhere.
crux.empirical: Then each camp points to its ledger: wage effects that may not survive capital adjusting; fiscal balances that differ by skill and generation; diversity’s link to trust that may not survive controls; and whether selection works or open movement scales.
crux.values: Then no ledger closes it; the question is whose losses count: a community’s right to its own size and character against a person’s claim not to be barred; the citizen at the bottom against the poorer stranger; shelter from persecution as duty or choice.

actions.title: Grade Congress with NumbersUSA
actions.description: Use NumbersUSA’s action board to see your member of Congress’s immigration-reduction grade and send them a message on current bills.

actions.title: Read Niskanen Center’s immigration research
actions.description: The Center’s case for reformed legal pathways sized to the workforce gaps employers report, as an alternative to both open borders and blanket restriction.

actions.title: Read British Future on immigration and integration
actions.description: An independent think tank engaging, in its own words, people’s hopes and fears about integration and immigration, identity and race; its attitudes tracker follows how the public actually moves as the numbers change.

actions.title: Support FWD.us’s immigration campaigns
actions.description: Follow FWD.us’s active fights to protect high-skilled visas and international student status from proposed restrictions, and its case for growing legal, economy-matched immigration.

actions.title: Donate to the International Rescue Committee
actions.description: Fund IRC resettlement, asylum and legal-integration programs; the IRC reports reaching more than 20.5 million people across more than 40 countries in 2025.

actions.title: Take action with United We Dream
actions.description: United We Dream describes itself as built and powered by immigrant youth; sign petitions, make calls and send texts on deportation defense, DACA and a path to citizenship.

actions.title: Back the Value Our Families campaign
actions.description: A coalition that says it works for a fairer, more efficient family immigration system, campaigning on the green-card backlog, per-country caps and the Reuniting Families Act.

actions.title: Sign the Project for Immigration Reform’s worker petitions
actions.description: The Institute for Sound Public Policy, which says it fights for Americans affected by immigration policy and offshoring, runs petitions on guest-worker visas and the displacement of US workers.

actions.title: Read WHO’s health workforce safeguards list
actions.description: WHO’s 2023 list of 55 countries whose health workforce is thin enough that it discourages active international recruitment from them, with the Global Code of Practice the list is built on.

actions.title: Read Migration that Works on temporary work visas
actions.description: The coalition, founded in 2011 as the International Labor Recruitment Working Group, publishes analysis of abuse across the H-2A, H-2B, H-1B, J-1 and TN visas and its own model for labor migration.

actions.title: Read Labor Mobility Partnerships on migration corridors
actions.description: LaMP states its purpose as creating better job opportunities for half a billion workers from low-income countries by 2050; its corridor projects and research set out what reliable, rights-respecting labor mobility would take.

actions.title: Read the case for open borders
actions.description: A reference site setting out the rights-based and utilitarian arguments that barring peaceful migration is unjust and forgoes trillions in global output.

actions.title: Read the border security agenda
actions.description: The Center for Renewing America’s case that a secure border and a labor market run for citizens first are one national-interest question, not two.

actions.title: Back PICUM’s undocumented-migrant campaigns
actions.description: PICUM is a network of organizations working for the rights of undocumented migrants in Europe, campaigning on regularization, worker protections, detention and deportation, and access to health care and justice.
